newsitem.title: USA: New U.S. Bosnia coordinator heads for Balkans.
newsitem.headline: New U.S. Bosnia coordinator heads for Balkans.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright named a new coordinator for U.S. policy toward Bosnia on Thursday and urged ethnic rivals there to intensify efforts to make their peace "self-sustaining."

Robert Gelbard departed several hours later on his first visit as coordinator to the Balkans, a 10-day trip that will include the highest-level U.S. talks with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic in five months.

Albright said the trip would "introduce Ambassador Gelbard to the parties in his new role and emphasise to the parties that we expect them to intensify their efforts to implement the Dayton agreement."

"We have much to do. Bosnia has been at peace for almost one-and-a-half years. It is time for the parties, with our help and within the structure of Dayton, to make the peace self-sustaining," she told a news briefing.

Saying it was critical for Bosnians to see the difference peace can make in their lives, she said efforts would be intensified to speed reconstruction, ensure that persons displaced by war can return home, that police function effectively and that war criminals are brought to justice.
These aspects of the 1995 Dayton Accords that ended the 1992-95 war in Bosnia are far from being implemented.

The adminstration has made clear its intention to withdraw U.S. troops from Bosnia when the mandate for the 31,000-strong NATO-led peacekeeping mission expires in mid-1998. It would be easier to do so if Bosnians live up to their peace deal.
On war criminals, Gelbard said the United States was deeply concerned that Bosnian Serbs and Croatia have not turned over war criminals to the Hague tribunal for trial.
But he played down a proposal to create a special military unit to nab suspects and bring them to The Hague. "I don't know anything about a special force...That is not an idea," he said.
He would concentrate on "pressing the parties" to comply with their Dayton Accords obligations but "we think that all options, ultimately, will have to be looked at in the future."
Gelbard was appointed by President Bill Clinton on Albright's recommendation. A career diplomat, he has been assistant secretary of state for international narcotics matters.

In that capacity, he was instrumental in confronting Colombian President Ernesto Samper with charges he took drug money for his election campaign and in deciding to de-certify Colombia as a country that cooperates with the United States in the fight against narcotics trafficking.

Gelbard takes over the Bosnia portfolio from John Kornblum, assistant secretary of state for European and Canadian affairs, who is expected to be nominated by Clinton to be the next ambassador to Germany.

In an apparent sign the coordinator's role is being elevated, Gelbard will have an office on the State Department's seventh floor, where Albright and top aides also have their offices. She said he would be U.S. "negotiator, coordinator and programme director for the Dayton accords."
In preparation for his new role, he has for some months had responsibility for U.S. efforts to build the international police force in Bosnia.

Washington had held regular meetings with Milosevic, a key signer of the Dayton Accords, but those ended after his government refused to recognise November elections won by the opposition and then cracked down on opposition protests.
Eventually in the face of domestic and international outrage, Milosevic was forced to back down.
Gelbard said he would press Milosevic to press the Bosnian Serbs to comply with all aspects of the Bosnia peace deal and also urge moves toward democracy in Serbia.

Gelbard and his team, including Kornblum, plan to visit Kosovo, a Serbian province that has suffered violent unrest as ethnic Albanians struggle for greater autonomy from Belgrade. They will also visit Croatia, Bosnia, and Macedonia.
